### 8.6 Quantitative FTA

The aim of quantitative FTA is the determination of some reliability and probabilistic parameters, mainly referred to the top event declared for the production system investigated. This analysis can be performed

Fig. 8.29 FTA, "reactor explosion." Configuration A - "redundancy." ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software


Fig. 8.30 Qualitative fault tree evaluation. EFT. Configuration A - "redundancy." ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software


Fig. 8.31 Equivalent reliability block diagram, "reactor explosion." Configuration A - "redundancy." ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software

Fig. 8.32 Equivalent reliability block diagram by the EFT. Configuration A - "redundancy." ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software


Fig. 8.33 FTA, "reactor explosion." Configuration B - "no redundancy." ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software


Fig. 8.34 Qualitative fault tree evaluation. EFT. Configuration B - "no redundancy." ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software
once MCS have been identified. It is a sequential evaluation which firstly determines the failure probability for the components, then the MCS, and finally the probabilities for the system, given the top event. The main equations for the determination of these probabilities are give as follows:

- Component failure probability. Generally, for any component, or basic primary event, a constant failure rate per hour is assumed, and any timedependent effect is ignored. If a generic component is considered, it could be necessary to distinguish a "standby failure rate" from an "operating failure rate": as a consequence, the proper failure rate has to be coupled to the proper time period, standbytime $t$ or operating time $t$, respectively. The component failure probability, which mainly refers to the nonrepairable items, is

$$
F_{j}(t)=F_{j, \mathrm{~s}}\left(t_{\mathrm{s}}\right)+\left[1-F_{j, \mathrm{~s}}\left(t_{\mathrm{s}}\right)\right] F_{j, \mathrm{o}}\left(t_{\mathrm{o}}\right)
$$

where s is the standby phase, $t_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the ready (i. e., standby) time period, o is the operating phase, and $t_{0}$ is the operating time period.
Assuming an exponential distribution for the random variable $t$, one can approximate the cumulated value $F(t)$ by its first-order term, when $\lambda t<0.1$, as follows:

$$
F(t) \cong \lambda t
$$

where $\lambda$ is the conditional and constant rate defined for the variable $t$.
In particular, if $t$ is the time to failure (ttf), then $F(t)$ is the failure probability function (unreliability) and $\lambda$ is the constant failure rate.
For repairable failures the constant asymptotic unavailability of a component is quantified by

$$
q_{j} \underset{\substack{\lambda=\text { constant } \\ \mu=\text { constant }}}{=} \frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}=\frac{\operatorname{MTTR} \times \lambda}{\mu} \underset{\mu \gg \lambda}{\cong} \frac{\lambda}{\mu}
$$

where $\mu$ is the repair rate.

- Failure probability and unavailability of a cut set given a top event. The general model for the evaluation of cut set unavailability, equivalent to failure probability, is

$$
q_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t)=\prod_{j \in \mathrm{CS}_{i}} q_{j}(t)
$$

where $\mathrm{CS}_{i}$ is cut set $i$ and $q_{j}(t)$ is the unavailability of component $j$ which belongs to $\mathrm{CS}_{i}$.

- Unavailability of the system given a top event.

$$
Q_{S}(t)=\coprod_{i} q_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t)=1-\prod_{i}\left[1-q_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t)\right]
$$

A simplified equation quantifying the unavailability of the system is

$$
Q_{S}(t) \cong \sum_{i} q_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t)
$$

- Component failure occurrence rate. This rate is defined for both repairable and nonrepairable components or systems. For nonrepairable items it is defined as

$$
w(t)=f(t)=\lambda \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

where $f(t)$ is the probability density function of the ttf.
For both unrepairable and repairable failures $\lambda(t)$ is a reasonable approximation of this rate.

- Failure occurrence rate of a cut set given a TOP event. A MCS failure occurs at time $t$ to $t+\Delta t$ if all components except one are down at time $t$, and the other component fails at time $t$ to $t+\Delta t$. Consequently,

$$
w_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t)=\sum_{j \in \mathrm{CS}_{i}} w_{j}(t) \prod_{\substack{k \neq j \\ k, j \in \mathrm{CS}_{i}}} q_{k}(t)
$$

where $w_{j}(t)$ is the failure rate of component $j$ in MCS $i$.

- ENF for a cut set. The ENF for a cut set $\mathrm{CS}_{i}$ on a time period $T$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ENF}_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T) & =W_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(0, T)=W_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T) \\
& =\int_{0}^{T} w_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t) \mathrm{d} t \\
& =\int_{0}^{T}\left(\sum_{j \in \mathrm{CS}_{i}} w_{j}(t) \prod_{\substack{k \neq j \\
k, j \in \mathrm{CS}_{i}}} q_{k}(t)\right) \mathrm{d} t
\end{aligned}
$$

where $T$ is the time period.

- ENF of a system on a time period T, given a top event.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{ENF}(T) & =W_{S}(T) \\
& =\sum_{i} W_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T)-\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\bigcap_{i} E\left(\mathrm{CS}_{i}\right)\right\} \\
& \leq \sum_{i} W_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\operatorname{Pr}\{\ldots\}$ is the failure probability and $E\left(\mathrm{CS}_{i}\right)$ is the failure event defined for cut set $i$.For the system the ENF is generally quantified by the following expression:

$$
\operatorname{ENF}(T) \cong \sum_{i} W_{\mathrm{C} S_{i}}
$$

- Virtual MTTR of a system given a top event. The following equations quantify the MTTR for the production system, given a top event:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{MTTR}_{S} & \cong \frac{Q_{S}(T)}{w_{s}(T)} \\
w_{s}(T) & =\frac{W_{s}(T)}{T}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $w_{s}(T)$ is the average estimated failure rate for the system.

### 8.6.1 Quantitative FTA, Numerical Example 1

The fault tree reported in Fig. 8.35 relates to a repairable system and five repairable components, or basic events, A, B, C, D, and E, having well-known failure and repair behaviors. The analyst needs to quantify the unavailability, the ENF, and the MTTR of the system for a given top event and assuming a period of time $T$ equal to $8,000 \mathrm{~h}$. Table 8.10 presents the values of the failure and repair rates assuming an exponential distribution, i. e., random failure and repair durations, for ttf and the time to repair ( ttr$)$.

By the application of the Boolean algebra, three MCS can be identified, each made up of two basic components:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{TOP} & =A B+A B E+A B D+A B C+E C+C D \\
& =A B+E C+C D
\end{aligned}
$$

The quantitative analysis of the fault tree is found on the values of availability and unavailability for each basic component illustrated in Table 8.11. In particular, the unavailability has been quantified by the application both of the simplified model in Eq. 8.11, as reported in the fourth column in Table 8.11, and the exact exponential analytical model illustrated in Chap. 5 (Eq. 5.83) as reported in the fifth column in Table 8.11. The reliability of the component, representing the survival function of the item to the first failure, has been quantified by the application of the simplified model [see Eq. 8.10 for the failure probability function $F(t)$ ], as reported in the sixth column in Table 8.11, and of


Fig. 8.35 Fault tree, numerical example 1
the exact model (see Eq. 5.27), as reported in the seventh column in Table 8.11.

Sometimes the simplified analytical models previously introduced are not applicable, as demonstrated by the value 2.4 assumed by the reliability for component C , while for other applications, such as for basic event D , the exact and simplified values of reliability significantly differ. A similar consideration can be made for the estimated values of availability.

Assuming the hypothesis of statistical independence between basic events related to the component of the system, the unavailabilities of the cut sets are

$$
\begin{aligned}
& q_{A B}=q_{\mathrm{A}} q_{\mathrm{B}} \cong 0.002 \times 0.0002 \cong 4 \times 10^{-7} \\
& q_{E C}=q_{\mathrm{E}} q_{\mathrm{C}} \cong 0.910 \times 0.08 \cong 0.073 \\
& q_{C D}=q_{\mathrm{C}} q_{\mathrm{D}} \cong 0.910 \times 0.002 \cong 1.82 \times 10^{-3}
\end{aligned}
$$

By application of Eq. 8.13, the unavailability of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{S}(8,000 \mathrm{~h})= & \bigsqcup_{i} q_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t) \\
= & 1-\left(1-4 \times 10^{-7}\right)(1-0.073) \\
& \times\left(1-1.82 \times 10^{-3}\right) \\
\cong & 0.0747
\end{aligned}
$$

If the simplified Eq. 8.14 is applied,

$$
Q_{S}(8,000 \mathrm{~h})=\sum_{i} q_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(t) \cong 0.0748
$$

In order to quantify the ENF of the system, Eq. 8.17 has been applied for each cut set:

$$
W_{\mathrm{CS}}(0,8,000)=\int_{0}^{8,000}\left(\sum_{i} w_{i}(t) \prod_{j \neq i} q_{j}(t)\right) \mathrm{d} t
$$

i.e.,

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{\mathrm{AB}}(0,8,000) & \cong \int_{0}^{T}\left[\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} q_{\mathrm{B}}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} q_{\mathrm{A}}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} t \\
& \cong \int_{0}^{8,000}\left[\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \tau_{\mathrm{B}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \tau_{\mathrm{A}}\right] \mathrm{d} t \\
& \cong\left[\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \tau_{\mathrm{B}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \tau_{\mathrm{A}}\right] \times 8,000 \\
& \cong 1.92 \times 10^{-4} \text { failures, }
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the MTTR of component B and $\tau_{\mathrm{A}}$ is the MTTR of component A , in accordance with the opportunity to apply the simplified analytical models of the unavailability.

Similarly, for the other cut sets,

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_{\mathrm{EC}}(T) & \cong \int_{0}^{T}\left[\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} q_{\mathrm{E}}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{E}} q_{\mathrm{C}}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} t \\
& \cong \lambda_{\mathrm{E}} \int_{0}^{T}\left[\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} t}\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} t\right] \mathrm{d} t \\
& \cong \lambda_{\mathrm{E}}\left(T+\left.\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{C}}}\left|\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} t}\right|_{0}^{T}+\frac{1}{2} \lambda_{\mathrm{C}} T^{2}\right)\right) \\
& \cong \lambda_{\mathrm{E}}\left(T+\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{C}}}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} T}-1\right)+\frac{1}{2} \lambda_{\mathrm{C}} T^{2}\right) \\
& \cong 10^{-5}\left(8,000+\frac{1}{3 \times 10^{-4}}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-8,000 \cdot 3 \cdot 10^{-4}}-1\right)\right. \\
& \left.\quad+0.5 \times 3 \times 10^{-4} \times 8,000^{2}\right) \\
\cong & 0.146 \text { failures, } \\
W_{\mathrm{CD}}(T) & \cong \int_{0}^{T}\left[\lambda_{\mathrm{D}} q_{\mathrm{C}}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} q_{\mathrm{D}}(t)\right] \mathrm{d} t \\
& \cong \lambda_{\mathrm{D}} \int_{0}^{T}\left[\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} t}\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} \tau_{\mathrm{D}}\right] \mathrm{d} t \\
& \cong \lambda_{\mathrm{D}}\left(T+\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{C}}}\left|\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} t}\right|_{0}^{T}+\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} \tau_{\mathrm{D}} T\right) \\
& \cong \lambda_{\mathrm{D}}\left(T+\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{C}}}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} T}-1\right)+\lambda_{\mathrm{C}} \tau_{\mathrm{D}} T\right) \\
& \cong 10^{-4}\left(8,000+\frac{1}{3 \times 10^{-4}}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-8000 \cdot 3 \cdot 10^{-4}}-1\right)\right. \\
& \left.\quad+3 \times 10^{-4} \frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-2}} \times 8,000\right) \\
\cong & 0.502 \text { failures. }
\end{aligned}
$$As a consequence, given the top event and assuming a period of time of $8,000 \mathrm{~h}$, the ENF for the system is

$$
\operatorname{ENF}(T) \cong \sum_{i} W_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}} \cong 0.648 \text { failures. }
$$

Now it is possible to quantify the MTTR of the system by the application of the Eq. 8.20:

$$
w_{S} \cong \frac{W_{S}(T)}{T}=\frac{0.648}{8000} \cong 8.1 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{MTTR}_{S} & =\frac{Q_{S}(T)}{\lambda_{s}(T)} \cong \frac{Q_{S}(T)}{w_{S}(T)} \\
& \cong \frac{0.0748}{8.1 \times 10^{-5}} \cong 923.5 \mathrm{~h}
\end{aligned}
$$

If the analyst has to quantify the failure probability of the repairable system considering the first failure, it is useful to evaluate the failure probabilities for the cut sets as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{A B}(T) & =F_{\mathrm{A}}(T) F_{\mathrm{B}}(T) \\
& \cong 0.148 \times 0.077 \cong 0.0114 \\
F_{E C}(T) & =q_{E C}=F_{\mathrm{E}}(T) F_{\mathrm{C}}(T) \\
& \cong 0.910 \times 0.077 \cong 0.070 \\
F_{C D}(T) & =F_{\mathrm{C}}(T) F_{\mathrm{D}}(T) \\
& \cong 0.910 \times 0.551 \cong 0.501
\end{aligned}
$$

The failure probability of the system $F_{S}(T)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{S}(8,000 \mathrm{~h})= & \coprod_{i} F_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T) \\
= & 1-(1-0.0114)(1-0.07) \\
& \times(1-0.501) \\
\cong & 0.541
\end{aligned}
$$

which is very similar to the "simplified" value:

$$
F_{S}(T=8,000 \mathrm{~h}) \cong \sum_{i} F_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T) \cong 0.582
$$

Figures 8.36 and 8.37 present the results obtained by the application of the Monte Carlo simulation analysis on the system for $T=8,000 \mathrm{~h}$. In particular, Fig. 8.36 shows the up/down diagram obtained for components/events A-E and their contributions. Component $C$ is clearly nonrepairable, but fortunately it is not a cut set and the system is always repairable within $8,000 \mathrm{~h}$.

For $T$ longer than $8,000 \mathrm{~h}$, the system can reach a state of nonrepairable failure owing to the simultaneous failure of the nonrepairable components E and C, as illustrated in Fig. 8.37.

Finally, Fig. 8.38 presents the histogram of the expected failures.

### 8.6.2.1 System Configuration A

The analytical evaluation of the reliability and the failure rate for the system, given a top event and assuming the redundant configuration A , is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{S}(t)= & R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) \times R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) \times R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& +R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \times R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) \times R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) \\
& -R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) \times R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) \times R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) \times R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \times R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
\lambda_{S}(t)= & \lambda_{\mathrm{P} 1 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\mathrm{PR} \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\text {no electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\mathrm{V} 1 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\mathrm{V} 2 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\mathrm{PR} \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\mathrm{PR} \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\text {no electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& +\lambda_{\mathrm{P} 2 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& -\lambda_{\mathrm{V} 2 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \\
& -\lambda_{\mathrm{V} 1 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \\
& -\lambda_{\mathrm{P} 1 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& -\lambda_{\mathrm{P} 2 \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& -\lambda_{\mathrm{PR} \text { broken }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\text {electric power }}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t) \\
& -\lambda_{\text {no electric power }}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 2}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 1}(t) R_{\mathrm{V} 2}(t) \\
& \times R_{\mathrm{PR}}(t) R_{\mathrm{P} 1}(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, during the simulation analysis a special counter would be required in order to get this value at $t^{*}$. This counter is incremented by one every time the system is up at $t^{*}$ considering the whole set of simulations runs; thus, the point availability at $t^{*}$ is
the number of times the system is up at $t^{*}$ divided by the number of simulation runs in the dynamic analysis. ### 8.7 Application 1 - FTA

This application deals with the FTA conducted on a heating plant for a $160-\mathrm{m}^{2}$ public lounge. The system, conventionally split into a hydronic device for warm water and a heating device based on water temperatures and thermic energy conservation, has three main components, as illustrated in the functional simplified block scheme of Fig. 8.59: the boiler, the distribution system (pumps, collectors, valves, etc.), and the heat exchangers. In particular, two fan-coils are fed in a redundant configuration, i. e., the heating system is supposed to be capable when at least one fan-coil is operating.

The hot water produced by the boiler is pumped by a force pump, called a "boiler pump," along a primary loop of piping; some thermic and hydraulic drops are obviously encountered. The hydraulic circuit is completed by a secondary loop, when the two heat exchangers in the controlled zone are fed by the same boiler, but it is possible to double the secondary loop (loop1 and loop2) in order to feed the fan-coils by two distinct and independent boiler systems. Each secondary loop is supported by its own pump. The generic loop associated with a boiler is made of two subloops, one for each exchanger. The environmental temperature is controlled by adjusting the hot water flow by means of automatic valves, one for each secondary loop, and a zone valve (mixing three-way valve) for each exchanger and for each loop. As a consequence, in the case of two fan-coils and two boilers, four valves are required. The boiler pump as well as every pump


Fig. 8.59 Functional block scheme of the thermic systemon the secondary loops operate according to the simultaneous and integrated control of sensors, such as a thermic sensor for each subloop, a flow fan temperature sensor for each fan, and an environmental sensor.

Some other critical components playing a significant role complete the generic FTA:

- a boiler system with natural gas adduction and combustion gas evacuation;
- two fan-coils;
- the electric power supply system;
- the water supply system with a hydraulic pipe adduction;
- the piping system, i. e., the piping distribution network;
- the hydraulic disjunctors, as many as the secondary loops, for the right mix of hot and cold water in the primary and secondary loops.

The hydraulic circuit has to be filled up with water at the start-up, and later the water recirculates in the system when it is working. A refill is sometimes required in order to compensate for some water leaks.

### 8.7.1 Fault Tree Construction

Assuming the situation "no thermic comfort" as the top event for the heating plant or "thermic system," one can develop some different fault trees in accordance with different system configurations and hypotheses. These trees are made of the four basic "subtrees" illustrated in Figs. 8.60-8.63, representing the events of absence of hot water within the two available fans as follows:


Fig. 8.60 Fault tree construction, subloop 1.1

Fig. 8.61 Fault tree construction, subloop 2.1

- Transfer out block 1.1. It refers to subloop 1.1, boiler 1 , and no hot water on fan 1.
- Transfer out block 2.1. It refers to subloop 2.1, boiler 2 (i. e., in the case of the existence of a second boiler), and no hot water on fan 1.
- Transfer out block 1.2. It refers to subloop 1.2, boiler 1 , and no hot water on fan 2.
- Transfer out block 2.2. It refers to subloop 2.2, boiler 2 (i. e., in the case of the existence of a second boiler), and no hot water on fan 2.

Every tree configuration, on five configurations A, $\mathrm{B}, \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{D}$, and E proposed, has been generated and analyzed from both a qualitative and a quantitative point of view as follows:

- Configuration $A$ - one boiler and fan-coil redundancy and fill water (Fig. 8.64.) There is only a single boiler and two redundant fan-coils, i. e., there is
one secondary loop made of two subloops, one for each fan. It is supposed the system requires the water supplier to be operative, i. e., in a state of function.
- Configuration B - one boiler and fan-coil redundancy (Fig. 8.65). There is only a single boiler and two redundant fan-coils, i. e., there is one secondary loop made of two subloops, one for each fan. It is also supposed the system does not require the water supplier to be operative because the piping has already been filled.
- Configuration $C$ - one boiler and no fan-coil redundancy (Fig. 8.66). There is only a single boiler and two fan coils, both necessary to guarantee thermic comfort. It is also supposed the system does not require the water supplier to be operative because the piping has already been filled.

Fig. 8.62 Fault tree construction, subloop 1.2

- Configuration $D$ - two boilers and fan-coil redundancy and fill water (Figs. 8.67 and 8.68). There are two alternative boilers (i.e., one is redundant) and two redundant fan-coils. It is also supposed the system requires the water supplier to be operative because the piping network could be empty.
- Configuration E - two boilers and fan-coil redundancy (Fig. 8.69). There are two alternative boilers (i.e., one is redundant) and two redundant fan-coils. It is also supposed the production system does not require the water supplier to be operative because the piping network is already filled (both primary and secondary loops).

The generic fault tree previously illustrated is made up of several blocks, many of which are primary blocks/events related to the components of the system investigated. Many blocks are mirrors of a few primary events, such as the so-called no electric power, the rupture on the "environmental thermic sensor," and the "no gas supply" event related to the natural gas supply system. The generic event mirror of a basic/primary component can be represented by a "little square" near the block associated with the event. The

### 8.7.3 Quantitative FTA

By the application of the analytical model illustrated in the previous sections of this chapter, it is possible to quantify the reliability parameters of the system, e.g., reliability $R_{S}(t)$ and MTTF. Table 8.16 summarizes these values for the five system configurations previously illustrated. In particular, the reliability function has been quantified for $t=4,000 \mathrm{~h}$ and
$t=6,570 \mathrm{~h}$, corresponding to an operating period of 1 year (i. e., 365 days per year and 18 h per day). The system is supposed to be nonrepairable and made up of nonrepairable components, and as a consequence these values refer to the first occurrence of the system failure event. In accordance with this hypothesis, the following sections illustrate some basic results obtained for the five system configurations previously introduced.

### 8.7.3.1 Configuration A - One Boiler and Fan-Coil Redundancy and Fill Water

### 8.8 Application 2 - FTA in a Waste to Energy System

This section introduces a case study including a costbased model for failure modes analysis, reliability prediction, and magnitude evaluation of a waste to energy (WtE) plant. The model pays particular attention to the economic determination and evaluation of the environmental effects, here called "externalities," of those facilities dedicated to the thermic treatment of waste, in accordance with the adoption of different maintenance policies. In detail, after a short description of the incinerator object of the study, this section illustrates the FTA conducted on some critical subsystems of the WtE plant.

A qualitative and quantitative evaluation of the solid waste incinerator is carried out and the results of these FTAs, as reported in Sects. 8.8.6 and 8.8.7, join in a cost-based prediction reliability model for the determination of the economic effects of the emissions, e.g., nitrogen oxides $\left(\mathrm{NO}_{x}\right)$ and carbon dioxide. This
model is based on the integration of a failure modes analysis, a reliability prediction analysis, and a "magnitude of consequences" evaluation, which takes inspiration from the large number of literature studies on the determination of the externalities in WtE plants.

### 8.8.1 Introduction to Waste Treatment

An incinerator is a waste treatment technology for the thermic treatment of waste. By high-temperature combustion it transforms waste into thermic energy useful for the generation of electricity and/or for district heating. An incinerator also produces gaseous emissions in the atmosphere and residual ash. The incinerator represents one of the most popular alternative technology to landfilling and biological treatment of waste. It is particularly popular in countries such as Japan where land is a scarce resource, but several municipalities all over the world, such as

Fig. 8.74 Failure rates of the system and of the most critical components. System configuration A. ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software

Hong Kong, Saugus in Massachusetts, USA, Brescia in Italy, London in the UK, and Tokyo in Japan, have adopted municipal solid waste incinerators. Table 8.18 presents a snapshot on WtE plants in Europe as of 2002.

A WtE plant is equipped with high-efficiency furnaces and devices for continuous monitoring of emissions and air pollution control. There are various types of incinerator plants:

- Simple incinerator made of a brick-lined cell, with a metal grate over a lower ash pit, and openings, called "clinkers," for waste loading and refuse removal; often used for domestic heating.
- Moving grate combustion. A grate enables the movement of waste through the combustion chamber.
- Rotary kiln, made of a long, slightly inclined cylindrical tube along which refuse is continuously moved and spills out of the end through the clink-
ers. The system is made of some different sections where waste is dried, ignited, and completely burned.
- Multiple/stepped heart. Waste is transported through the furnace by moving teeth mounted on a central rotating shaft.
- Fluidized bed. An flow of air is forced through a bed of sand. The sand particles separate, enabling air to flow through; thus, a fluidized bed is created and fuel and waste can be introduced. The mass of waste, fuel, and sand is fully circulated through the furnace.


### 8.8.2 Case study

The WtE plant considered, as reported in Table 8.19, has a plant capacity, or waste treatment capacity, of about 200 ton/day for $2,600 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}$

Fig. 8.76 Static reliability analysis. System configuration B. ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software
of waste, resulting in $11,000 \mathrm{MWh} /$ year of electric energy and $34,000 \mathrm{MWh} /$ year of thermic energy produced, thus corresponding to 1.238 kWh for each kilogram of waste. The system supplies thermic energy for a community of about 2,600 families.

### 8.8.3 Emissions and Externalities: Literature Review

Even incinerators are faced with environmental and health questions. An exemplifying list obtained from the literature mentions damage to buildings, forests,

Fig. 8.77 Time-dependent reliability analysis. System configuration B. ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software
and agricultural yields; costs associated with transportation and logistics (e.g., vehicle emissions, congestion, accidents, noise); odor, dust, visual intrusion, etc. The magnitude of these effects strongly depends on the distance from the site, the type of waste, topography, prevailing wind directions, etc., and as a consequence the costs of externalities can range in a wide interval.

According to EC Directives, published in 2000, $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ emissions, with about $70 \%$ of the total health costs, are the most critical externality generated by an incinerator. They are believed to aggravate asthmatic conditions, and react with the oxygen in the air to produce ozone, which is also an irritant, and eventually forming nitric acid when they are dissolved in water. When they are dissolved in atmospheric moisture, the result is acid rain, which can damage entire forest ecosystems.

As illustrated in Table 8.20, costs associated with $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ vary very significantly in literature studies (Eshet et al. 2006), ranging from US $\$ 0.13$ to US $\$ 18.6$
per kilogram of $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$. This table presents economic unit values of all externalities associated with different emissions $\left(\mathrm{CO}_{2}, \mathrm{CH}_{4}, \mathrm{NO}_{x}, \mathrm{PM}_{10}, \mathrm{SO}_{2}\right.$, etc.) for both landfill and incinerators. These economic unit values are quantified in dollar per kilogram of pollutant (at 2003 prices). Table 8.21 reports economic valuations in US dollars per ton of waste (2003 prices) for specific impacts (e.g., transportation, leachate) for incineration.

The following analysis and results refer to the control and reduction of $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ emissions in the incinerator considered, with particular attention to the so-called selective noncatalytic reduction (SNCR) technology.

### 8.8.4 SNCR Plant

Table 8.22 quantifies the annual cost of externalities associated with some critical emissions of the incinerator, in accordance with the economic unit values

Fig. 8.78 Failure rates of the system and of the most critical components. System configuration B. ReliaSoft ${ }^{\circledR}$ software
collected from the literature (total average value in Table 8.20, last row). In particular, the emission of $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ represents about $33.5 \%$ of the admissible value of $85.619 \mathrm{~kg} /$ year (EC Directives); moreover, the related cost represents $99 \%$ of global social costs associated with pollutant emissions.

In order to limit gas emissions in the atmosphere, and in particular the emissions of $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$, in accordance with the limits fixed by 2000/76/CE Directive, a SNCR plant has been recently introduced. The SNCR technology injects urea into the firebox of the boiler to react with the nitrogen oxides formed in the combustion process at a gas temperature between 1,600 and $2,100^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$. This chemical reaction produces elemental nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and water. As a result of the introduction of the SNCR plant, the average value of $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ emissions decreased from 150 to $120 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}$. This is the control parameter of the incineration process, and values greater than $200 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}$, as declared by the manufacturer, can reveal anomalies.

Figure 8.94 illustrates the statistical distribution of $\mathrm{NO}_{x}\left(\mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}\right)$ emissions during a period of time $T$ from June 2005 to February 2007, for the power plant considered. This analysis is based on more than 25,000 half-hour observations. A half-hourly observation gives the average value of 30 values registered each minute.

Figure 8.95 reports the trend of half-hour values during the 20 -month observation period. By an in-depth analysis of these values, for $12,185 \mathrm{~h}$ the $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ emissions did not pass the critical value of $200 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}$, while for 75 h the SNCR system did not function correctly. In particular, the emission values exceeded $235 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}$ for 4 h .

Nevertheless this equation is not correct because the absorption laws can be applied only in the case when the same basic component event, i. e., the same item, is redundant in a Boolean equation. For example, if components DH51001 and DH51002 have the same failure behavior but they deal with distinct items, the following reduction is consequently false:

In the same way the other reductions in the equation reported above are not feasible. The basic events involved are not mirror ${ }^{1}$ items.

### 8.8.7 $\mathrm{NO}_{\mathrm{x}}$ Emissions: Quantitative FTA Evaluation

This section summarizes the results obtained by the evaluation of the most important reliability parameters related to the system, given a specific top event "exceeding $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ limit." For this purpose, Table 8.23 summarizes some significant parameters for the basic/primary components of the system which are involved in MCS previously identified. In particular,
assuming a length of the period of time $T$ equal to 365 h , about 15 days, the approximated values of the unavailability by Eq. 8.11 and of the probability function $F(T)$ by Eq. 8.10 are reported in Table 8.23, columns 4 and 5, respectively, while the exact value of $F(T)$ is in the last column.

In order to properly illustrate the correct quantitative evaluation of the fault trees in Figs. 8.96 and 8.100, the analysis is conducted on MCS assuming the same failure behavior for every component of the same kind, i. e., pumps, filters, and spears. Similarly, the failure probability function of the system for the period of time $T$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{S}(t=T) & =\coprod_{i} F_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T)=1-\prod_{i}\left[1-F_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T)\right] \\
& =0.08373 \leq \sum_{i} F_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}}(T) \cong 0.08665
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Eq. 8.18, the ENF for the system is
$\operatorname{ENF}(T=365 \mathrm{~h}) \cong \sum_{i} W_{\mathrm{CS}_{i}} \cong 7.25 \times 10^{-2}$ failures.
Finally, the MTTR defined for the system, given the top event, can be quantified by the application of

Eq. 8.20:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{MTTR}_{S} & \cong \frac{Q_{S}(T)}{w_{s}(T)}=\frac{7.412 \times 10^{-4}}{1.986 \times 10^{-4}} \cong 3.73 \mathrm{~h} \\
w_{s}(T) & =\frac{W_{s}(T)}{T}=\frac{0.0725}{365} \\
& \cong 1.986 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{day}^{-1}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

design and to put in light the most critical component failures for the system. They can assist in identifying the fault tree event whose upgrade is most likely to yield the greatest improvement in system performance. These measures are:

- Birnbaum. It determines the maximum increase of the risk due to the failure event of a component in comparison with when the component is operating. This measure is very important because it allows one to rate how much the top gate probability changes when the unavailability of a basic event has changed; as a consequence, it is possible to rank the events according to the Birnbaum measure and to select those on which to concentrate the best efforts for improvement. The Birnbaum measure is defined
as follows:

$$
I_{\mathrm{B}}(A)=P(\operatorname{TOP} \backslash A)-P(\operatorname{TOP} \backslash \bar{A})
$$

where $A$ is the primary/basic event and TOP is the top event.

- Criticality. The criticality importance measure of event A determines the probability that the top event, here assumed to have occurred, is due to the failure of component A :

$$
I_{\mathrm{C}}(A)=I_{\mathrm{B}}(A) \frac{P(A)}{P(\mathrm{TOP})}
$$

- Fussell-Vesely. Given that the system failed, the Fussell-Vesely measure determines the probability

Fig. 8.94 Distribution of $\mathrm{NO}_{X}$ emission values. Year 2006 (25,091 half-hour observations)


Fig. 8.95 Half-hour values of $\mathrm{NO}_{X}$ emissions $\left(\mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{Nm}^{3}\right)$
that component A contributed to this failure. In particular, it is the ratio of the probability of occurrence of any cut set containing event $A$ and the probability of the top event.

The Birnbaum importance measure considers only the conditional probability that event $A$ is critical, while the criticality importance measure also takes into account the overall probability of the occurrence of the top event due to event $A$.

According to this criticality analysis, the urea tank, electric equipment, and air secondary piping are the most critical parts.

### 8.8.9 Spare Parts Availability, What-If Analysis

As illustrated in Fig. 8.96, the system unavailability for a period of time $T$ equal to 365 h is $7.407 \times 10^{-4}$; for a longer period of 1 year the availability of the
system, given the top event, is 0.9984 , as reported in the second column of Table 8.25 . This last value was obtained by the application of the Monte Carlo dynamic simulation with 10,000 repetitions, i. e., simulating the failures and repair events for 10,000 virtual production systems based on the same components/basic events parameterization. The point availability $A(t)$ at $t=8,760 \mathrm{~h}$ is about 0.9979 , while the reliability is about 0.1735 for a mission period $T$ $\left(=t-t_{0}\right)$ equal to 1 year. Other significant results, reported in Table 8.25, are the ENF, the mean time to first failure, and the annual downtime, which amounts to $13.74 \mathrm{~h} /$ year. This system configuration is called "optimistic" because it does not consider the lead times required to supply spare parts, such as valves and pumps, in the case of failures and corrective maintenance actions. In other words, the MTTR is based on the optimistic hypothesis of assured availability of every generic spare part, i. e., a fulfillment lead time equal to zero or an infinite number of spare parts in storage.

### 8.8.10 System Modifications for ENF Reduction and Effects Analysis

This section exemplifies the impacts on reliability and costs associated with some modifications to the SNCR plant and to the strategies/rules for the control of $\mathrm{NO}_{x}$ emissions. In particular, they deal with the introduction of two alternative management policies for the critical valve VR1101. Similar considerations could of course be applied to other parts and components of the system.

### 8.8.10.1 A Redundant Valve

In the case of insertion of a new redundant valve in a parallel configuration, the fault tree changes. In Table 8.26 the performance of the system and the related externality costs are compared for different configurations/parameterizations, assum-
ing a planning period $T=8,760 \mathrm{~h}$; the total amount of the annual cost saving, due to the introduction of a second redundant valve, for three scenarios is:

1. Optimistic configuration,

$$

& \quad=126,675-183,066 \\
& \quad=-\mathrm{US} \$ 56,391 \text { per year }(-30.8 \%)

$$

2. Realistic configuration,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Delta \text { Cost }_{\text {extern_annual }} \text { (real.) } \\

& \quad=156,288-383,308 \\
& \quad=-\mathrm{US} \$ 227,020 \text { per year }(-59.2 \%)

It is worth noting that the redundant valve brings very important benefits from an environmental and social point of view; moreover, this introduction is very profitable, considering an annual investment cost of about $\$ 6,000$. ### 8.9 Markov Analysis and Time-Dependent Components/Systems

Markov modeling and analysis are very useful in the presence of dependences among basic/primary events in a fault tree, in particular with standby redundancies and common causes. A Markov chain is a discretetime stochastic process complying with the so-called Markov property: given the present state of a system/component, its future states are independent of its past states. Alternatively stated, the present state description fully captures all the information that can influence the future evolution of the process. Thus, given the present, the future is conditionally independent of the past. In particular, at the generic time instant the system may change its state from the current state to another state, or it may remain in the same state, according to a certain probability distribution. These changes of state are called "transitions," and the probabilities associated with various state changes are termed "transition probabilities."

Formally given a sequence of random variables $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots$ with the Markov property, the future
and past states are independent:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P\left\{X_{n+1}=x \backslash X_{n}=x_{n}, \ldots, X_{1}=x_{1}\right\} \\
& \quad=P\left\{X_{n+1}=x \backslash X_{n}=x_{n}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

The state space of the chain is the set of possible values assumed by $X_{i}$. Markov chains are often described by a directed graph, where the edges are labeled by the probabilities of going from one state to the other states, as illustrated in Fig. 8.101.

In other words, considering a generic system, $S_{i}\left(t_{i}\right)$ identifies the state $S_{i}$ of the system at the instant of time $t_{i}$ and Eq. 8.21 changes as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P\left\{S_{n+1}\left(t_{n}+\Delta t\right) \backslash S_{n}\left(t_{n}\right), S_{n-1}\left(t_{n-1}\right), \ldots, S_{1}\left(t_{1}\right)\right\} \\
& \quad=P\left\{S_{n+1}\left(t_{n}+\Delta t\right) \backslash S_{n}\left(t_{n}\right)\right\}=P_{n, n+1}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $P_{n, n+1}$ represents the transition from state $n$ to state $n+1$.

The generic Markov chain can be modeled by a set of differential equations, in accordance with the notation introduced in Fig. 8.101. Given a state $i$ for the system and transitions $t_{k}$ and $t_{j}$, respectively, from

Fig. 8.101 Markov chain and differential equation model
state $i$ to state $k$ and from state $j$ to state $i$,

$$
P_{i}(t+\Delta t)=P_{i}(t)\left(1-t_{k} \Delta t\right)+P_{j}(t) t_{j} \Delta t
$$

Equation 8.23 can be explained as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{i}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} & =\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{P_{i}(t+\Delta t)-P_{i}(t)}{\Delta t} \\
& =P_{j}(t) t_{j}-P_{i}(t) t_{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

In general,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{i}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\sum_{j \in\{\text { state } \mathrm{IN} i\}} P_{j}(t) t_{j}-\sum_{k \in\{\text { state OUT } i\}} P_{i}(t) t_{k}
$$

when

$$
\sum_{j \in\{\text { state of the system } S\}} P_{j}(t)=1
$$

### 8.9.1 Redundant Parallel Systems

A significant example of the Markov chain theory is its application to the reliability prediction for a system made of two components, A and B , in a parallel configuration. For each component, consider the two states of function $\{0,1\}$, representing the state of function or of failure, respectively; typical notation is reported schematically in Fig. 8.102.

Figure 8.103 presents the Markov chain model, based on a vertex made of three sections as in Fig. 8.102, for a parallel system made of nonrepairable components $\left(\mu_{\mathrm{A}}=\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=0\right)$.

Functioning components


Fig. 8.102 Vertex sections in the graph representation of a Markov chain


Fig. 8.103 Markov chain for a parallel system and nonrepairable components

By the application of Eq. 8.25,

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=-P_{1}(t)\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=P_{1}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}-P_{2}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \\
\frac{\mathrm{~d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=P_{1}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}-P_{3}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \\
\frac{\mathrm{~d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=P_{2}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+P_{3}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}
\end{array}\right.
$$

considering the following starting conditions:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
P_{1}(0)=1 \\
P_{j}(0)=0 \quad \forall j \neq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$

where 1,2 , etc. refer to states $S_{1}, S_{2}$, etc. (see Fig. 8.103).

By the application of the Laplace transform,

$$
F(s)=L[y(t)]=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{e}^{-s t} y(t) \mathrm{d} t
$$and the following property

$$
L\left[\frac{\mathrm{~d} y(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}\right]=s F(s)-y\left(t=0^{+}\right)
$$

to Eq. 8.27,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
s p_{1}-1 & =-p_{1}\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \\
s p_{2} & =p_{1} \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}-p_{2} \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \\
s p_{3} & =p_{1} \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}-p_{3} \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \\
s p_{4} & =p_{2} \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} p_{3}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Other general and useful analytical relationships and properties are

$$
\begin{aligned}
L[f(t)] & =F(s) \\
L[1] & =\frac{1}{s} \\
L[k] & =\frac{k}{s} \\
L[t] & =\frac{1}{s^{2}} \\
L\left[\mathrm{e}^{-k t}\right] & =\frac{1}{s+k} \\
L^{-1}[F(s)] & =f(t)
\end{aligned}
$$

As a consequence, it is useful to derive from Eq. 8.26 the following equation:

$$
p_{4}=\frac{1}{s}-p_{1}-p_{2}-p_{3}
$$

From Eqs. 8.30 and 8.31 the values of $p_{i}(s)$ are

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
p_{1}(s) & =\frac{1}{s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)}=\frac{P_{1}(s)}{Q_{1}(s)} \\
p_{2}(s) & =\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}} p_{1}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}} \frac{1}{s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)} \\
& =\frac{P_{2}(s)}{Q_{2}(s)} \\
p_{3}(s) & =\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}} p_{1}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}} \frac{1}{s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)} \\
& =\frac{P_{3}(s)}{Q_{3}(s)} \\
& \quad\left[s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)\right]\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\right) \\
& \quad-s\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\right) \\
p_{4}(s) & =\frac{-\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} s\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\right)-\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} s\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)}{s\left[s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)\right]\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\right)} \\
& =\frac{P_{4}(s)}{Q_{4}(s)}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The inverse Laplace transform is then applied in accordance with the following property:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L^{-1}\left[\frac{P(s)}{Q(s)}\right]= & \phi\left(a_{1}\right) \mathrm{e}^{a_{1} t}+\phi\left(a_{2}\right) \mathrm{e}^{a_{2} t} \\
& +\cdots+\phi\left(a_{n}\right) \mathrm{e}^{a_{n} t}
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
\phi(s)=\frac{(s-a) P(s)}{Q(s)}
$$

and $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}$ are nonmultiple roots of $Q(s)=0$.
The roots obtained in Eq. 8.32 when $Q(s)=0$ are

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
a_{1} & =-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \\
\phi\left(s=a_{1}\right) & =\frac{\left(s-a_{1}\right) P(s)}{Q(s)}=1
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

As a consequence,

$$
P_{1}(t)=L^{-1}\left[\frac{P(s)}{Q(s)}\right]=\phi\left(a_{1}\right) \mathrm{e}^{a_{1} t}=\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) t}
$$

Exactly the same result can be obtained by the integration of the first term in Eq. 8.27:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{P_{1}(t)} & =-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} t \\
\int_{P_{1}(0)}^{P_{1}(t)} \frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{P_{1}(t)} & =-\int_{0}^{t}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \mathrm{d} t \\
\ln \left[P_{1}(t)\right] & =-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) t \\
P_{1}(t) & =\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) t}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This result is the well-known expression of the reliability of a serial system made of unrepairable components as illustrated in Sect. 6.4. In fact, in state 1 components A and B have to be in a state of function.Similarly, we have the expression for $P_{2}(t)$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{1}=-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \\
& a_{2}=-\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \\
& \phi\left(s=a_{1}\right)=\frac{\left(s-a_{1}\right) P_{2}(s)}{Q_{2}(s)} \\
& =\left[s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)\right] \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}} \frac{1}{s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)} \\
& =\left.\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}}\right|_{s=-}\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)=-1 \\
& \phi\left(s=a_{2}\right)=\frac{\left(s-a_{2}\right) P_{2}(s)}{Q_{2}(s)} \\
& =\left(s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}} \frac{1}{s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)} \\
& =\left.\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}}{s+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right)}\right|_{s=-\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}}=1 \\
& P_{2}(t)=L^{-1}\left[\frac{P_{2}(s)}{Q_{2}(s)}\right] \\
& =\phi\left(a_{1}\right) \mathrm{e}^{a_{1} t}+\phi\left(a_{2}\right) \mathrm{e}^{a_{2} t} \\
& =\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} t}-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) t} .
\end{aligned}
$$

In the same way we obtain $P_{3}(t)$ and $P_{4}(t)$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{3}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} t}-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) t} \\
& P_{4}(t)=1-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} t}-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} t}+\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) t}
\end{aligned}
$$

By the calculus of $1-P_{4}(t)$ it is possible to evaluate the reliability of a parallel redundant system as illustrated in Sect. 6.5.

### 8.9.2 Parallel System with Repairable Components

This section applies the Markov chain modeling to the analysis of a parallel system made up of repairable components, as illustrated in Fig. 8.104. In particular, it is assumed that it is not possible to return to state $S_{2}$ or $S_{3}$, starting from $S_{4}$. The main aim of this analysis


Fig. 8.104 Markov chain for a parallel system and repairable components
is the determination of $P_{1}$ :

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\mu_{\mathrm{A}} P_{2}(t)+\mu_{\mathrm{B}} P_{3}(t)-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{1}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=P_{1}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\mu_{\mathrm{A}}\right) P_{2}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=P_{1}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{3}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=P_{3}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+P_{2}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \\
P_{1}(0)=1 \\
P_{j}(0)=0, \quad j \neq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$

Applying Laplace transforms,

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
s p_{1}-1=\mu_{\mathrm{A}} p_{2}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}} p_{3}-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}\right) p_{1} \\
s p_{2}=\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} p_{1}-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\mu_{\mathrm{A}}\right) p_{2} \\
s p_{3}=\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} p_{1}-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) p_{3} \\
p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3}+p_{4}=\frac{1}{s}
\end{array}\right.
$$

As a consequence,

$$
p_{1}=\frac{1}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}-\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \mu_{\mathrm{A}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\mu_{\mathrm{A}}}-\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \mu_{\mathrm{B}}}{s+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}}}
$$

Fig. 8.105 Probability of the event "system in state $S_{1}$ "

Applying the inverse Laplace transform in the special case $\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}=\lambda$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{A}}=\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=\mu$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{1}(t)= & L^{-1}\left[p_{1}(s)\right] \\
= & \frac{\left[-\frac{1}{2} \lambda+\frac{1}{2} \mu+\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\lambda^{2}+6 \lambda \mu+\mu^{2}}\right]}{\left[-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{t}\left(3 \lambda+\mu-\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+6 \lambda \mu+\mu^{2}}\right)\right]} \\
& \sqrt{\lambda^{2}+6 \lambda \mu+\mu^{2}} \\
& \left[\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{\lambda^{2}+6 \lambda \mu+\mu^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}(\lambda-\mu)\right] \\
& +\frac{\exp \left[-\frac{1}{2} t\left(\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+6 \lambda \mu+\mu^{2}}+3 \lambda+\mu\right)\right]}{\sqrt{\lambda^{2}+6 \lambda \mu+\mu^{2}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, it is possible to quantify $P_{2}(t)$ and $P_{3}(t)$.
Figure 8.105 presents the probability that the system is in state 1.

In the case of repairable component A and/or component B and in the state of failure of both (see state $S_{4}$ in Fig. 8.106), it could be useful to quantify the unavailability of the system, which is equal to the probability $P_{4}(t)$, i. e., the availability:

$$
A(t)=1-P_{4}(t)
$$



Fig. 8.106 Markov chain for a parallel system and repairable components

The differential equation related to state $S_{4}$ is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=P_{3}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+P_{2}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{B}}-\left(\mu_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{4}(t)
$$### 8.9.3 Standby Parallel Systems

In this section different examples regarding repairable systems are illustrated in accordance with the new notation reported in Fig. 8.107.

Figure 8.108 represents the Markov chain model of the standby parallel system when the generic component, in the standby state, is not subject to failures. This is the so-called cold standby parallel system. Similarly, Fig. 8.109 presents the Markov chain model of the system when the generic standby component C can fail, with failure rate $\lambda_{\mathrm{C}}^{\prime}$, during the "waiting time": this is a "warm standby" parallel system.

### 8.9.3.1 Cold Standby

In the cold standby parallel system (Fig. 8.108),

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\mu_{\mathrm{B}} P_{3}(t)-P_{1}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} \\
\frac{\mathrm{~d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\mu_{\mathrm{A}} P_{4}(t)-P_{2}(t) \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} \\
\frac{\mathrm{~d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} P_{2}(t)+\mu_{\mathrm{A}} P_{5}(t)-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{3}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} P_{1}(t)+\mu_{\mathrm{B}} P_{5}(t)-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\mu_{\mathrm{A}}\right) P_{4}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{5}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} P_{3}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} P_{4}(t)-\left(\mu_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{5}(t) \\
P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t)+P_{5}(t)=1 \\
P_{1}(0)=1 \\
P_{j}(0)=0, \quad j \neq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$

Cold stand-by


Fig. 8.107 Vertex sections in the graph representation of a Markov chain

In the case of $\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}=\lambda$ and $\mu_{\mathrm{A}}=\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=\mu$,

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\mu P_{3}(t)-P_{1}(t) \lambda \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\mu P_{4}(t)-P_{2}(t) \lambda \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda P_{2}(t)+\mu P_{5}(t)-(\lambda+\mu) P_{3}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda P_{1}(t)+\mu P_{5}(t)-(\lambda+\mu) P_{4}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{5}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda\left[P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t)\right]-2 \mu P_{5}(t) \\
P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t)+P_{5}(t)=1 \\
P_{1}(0)=1 \\
P_{j}(0)=0, \quad j \neq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$



Fig. 8.108 Markov chain for a parallel cold standby system


Fig. 8.109 Markov chain for a parallel warm standby systemIt is now possible to define three new states for the system as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
P_{0}(t) & =P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t) \\
P_{\mathrm{I}}(t) & =P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t) \\
P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) & =P_{5}(t)
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Then,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{0}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} & =\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}+\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} \\
& =\mu\left[P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t)\right]-\left[P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)\right] \lambda \\
& =\mu P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)-P_{0}(t) \lambda \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} & =\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}+\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} \\
& =\lambda P_{0}(t)+2 \mu P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)-(\lambda+\mu) P_{\mathrm{I}}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} & =\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{5}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda P_{I}(t)-2 \mu P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) \\
P_{0}(t)+P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)+P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) & =1 \\
P_{\mathrm{I}}(0)=1 \\
P_{j}(0) & =0, \quad j \neq \mathrm{I}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

By the application of Laplace transforms,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
s p_{0}-1 & =\mu p_{\mathrm{I}}-p_{0} \lambda \\
s p_{\mathrm{I}} & =p_{0} \lambda-p_{\mathrm{I}}(\lambda+\mu)+2 \mu p_{\mathrm{II}} \\
s p_{\mathrm{II}} & =\lambda p_{\mathrm{I}}-2 \mu p_{\mathrm{II}} \\
p_{0}+p_{\mathrm{I}} & +p_{\mathrm{II}}=1 / s
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

As a consequence,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
p_{0} & =\frac{\left(s^{2}+3 \mu s+s \lambda+2 \mu^{2}\right)}{s\left(s^{2}+2 s \lambda+3 \mu s+2 \mu \lambda+\lambda^{2}+2 \mu^{2}\right)} \\
p_{\mathrm{I}} & =\frac{\lambda(s+2 \mu)}{s^{3}+2 \lambda s^{2}+3 \mu s^{2}+2 \lambda \mu s+\lambda^{2} s+2 \mu^{2} s} \\
p_{\mathrm{II}} & =\frac{\lambda^{2}}{s\left(s^{2}+2 \lambda s+3 \mu s+2 \mu \lambda+\lambda^{2}+2 \mu^{2}\right)}
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

It is possible to quantify the probability of the system being in states $S_{0}, S_{\mathrm{I}}$, and $S_{\mathrm{II}}$, by the application of the inverse Laplace transform to $p_{0}, p_{\mathrm{I}}$, and $p_{\mathrm{II}}$. In particular, the state of not function is quantified by the
following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)= \\
& \sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)}-\sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)} \\
& \lambda^{2} \frac{\times \exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} t(3 \mu+2 \lambda)\right) \cosh \left(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{t} \sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)}\right)}{\left(\lambda^{2}+2 \mu^{2}+\lambda \mu\right) \sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)}} \\
& -3 \lambda^{2} \mu \frac{\exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} t(3 \mu+2 \lambda)\right) \sinh \left(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{t} \sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)}\right)}{\left(\lambda^{2}+2 \mu^{2}+\lambda \mu\right) \sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)}} \\
& -2 \lambda^{3} \frac{\exp \left(-\frac{1}{2} t(3 \mu+2 \lambda)\right) \sinh \left(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{t} \sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)}\right)}{\left(\lambda^{2}+2 \mu^{2}+\lambda \mu\right) \sqrt{\mu(\mu+4 \lambda)}}
\end{aligned}
$$

while the state of function is

$$
1-P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)
$$

Figure 8.110 presents the trend of the probability $P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)$ assuming $\lambda=10^{-4}$ (unit of time) ${ }^{-1}$ and $\mu=$ $10^{-3}$ (unit of time) ${ }^{-1}$.

### 8.9.3.2 Warm Standby

In the warm standby parallel system (Fig. 8.109),

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\mu_{\mathrm{B}} P_{3}(t)-P_{1}(t)\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime}\right) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\mu_{\mathrm{A}} P_{4}(t)-P_{2}(t)\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}^{\prime}\right) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} P_{2}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime} P_{1}(t)+\mu_{\mathrm{A}} P_{5}(t) \\
-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{3}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} P_{1}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime} P_{2}(t)+\mu_{\mathrm{B}} P_{5}(t) \\
-\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\mu_{\mathrm{A}}\right) P_{4}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{5}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda_{\mathrm{A}} P_{3}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} P_{4}(t)-\left(\mu_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{5}(t) \\
P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t)+P_{5}(t)=1 \\
P_{1}(0)=1 \\
P_{j}(0)=0, \quad j \neq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$

Fig. 8.110 Failure probability of the standby system ("system in state II")

In the case of $\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}=\lambda, \mu_{\mathrm{A}}=\mu_{\mathrm{B}}=\mu$, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}^{\prime}=\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime}=\lambda^{\prime}$,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \mu_{\mathrm{B}} P_{3}(t)-P_{1}(t)\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime}\right) \\
= & \mu P_{3}(t)-P_{1}(t)\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \mu_{\mathrm{A}} P_{4}(t)-P_{2}(t)\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}^{\prime}\right) \\
= & \mu P_{4}(t)-P_{2}(t)\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \lambda_{\mathrm{B}} P_{2}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime} P_{1}(t)+\mu_{\mathrm{A}} P_{5}(t) \\
& -\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{3}(t) \\
= & \lambda P_{2}(t)+\lambda^{\prime} P_{1}(t)+\mu P_{5}(t) \\
& -(\lambda+\mu) P_{3}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{4}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} P_{1}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime} P_{2}(t)+\mu_{\mathrm{B}} P_{5}(t) \\
& -\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+\mu_{\mathrm{A}}\right) P_{4}(t) \\
= & \lambda P_{1}(t)+\lambda^{\prime} P_{2}(t)+\mu P_{5}(t) \\
& -(\lambda+\mu) P_{4}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{5}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \lambda_{\mathrm{A}} P_{3}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}} P_{4}(t)-\left(\mu_{\mathrm{A}}+\mu_{\mathrm{B}}\right) P_{5}(t) \\
= & \lambda P_{3}(t)+\lambda P_{4}(t)-2 \mu P_{5}(t) \\
P_{1}(t)+ & P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t)+P_{5}(t)=1 \\
P_{1}(0)= & 1 \\
P_{j}(0)= & 0, \quad j \neq 1
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In particular, it is possible to define three new states for the system as follows:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
P_{0}(t) & =P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t) \\
P_{\mathrm{I}}(t) & =P_{3}(t)+P_{4}(t) \\
P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) & =P_{5}(t)
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The unavailability of the system is quantified by $P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)$ :

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{0}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \mu P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)-P_{0}(t)\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right) P_{0}(t)-(\lambda+\mu) P_{\mathrm{I}}(t) \\
& +2 \mu P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}= & \lambda P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)-2 \mu P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) \\
P_{0}(t)+ & P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)+P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)=1 \\
P_{0}(0)= & 1 \\
P_{j}(0)= & 0, j \neq 0
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

By the application of Laplace transforms,

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
s p_{0}-1 & =\mu p_{\mathrm{I}}-p_{0}\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
s p_{\mathrm{I}} & =p_{0}\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)-p_{\mathrm{I}}(\lambda+\mu)+2 \mu p_{\mathrm{II}} \\
s p_{\mathrm{II}} & =\lambda p_{I}-2 \mu p_{\mathrm{II}} \\
p_{0}+p_{\mathrm{I}} & +p_{\mathrm{II}}=1 / s
\end{aligned}\right.
$$Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathrm{I}}= & \frac{\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)(s+2 \mu)}{s^{3}+3 \mu s^{2}+2 \lambda s^{2}+2 \lambda \mu s+\lambda^{\prime} s^{2}} \\
& +2 \lambda^{\prime} \mu s+s \lambda^{2}+s \lambda \lambda^{\prime}+2 \mu^{2} s
\end{aligned}
$$

The probability of the system being in a state of function, but with a component under repair, can be quantified by the application of the inverse Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)\left(-\mu \sqrt{\lambda^{\prime 2}-2 \lambda^{\prime} \mu+\mu^{2}+4 \lambda \mu}\right. \\
\left.-\mu^{2}+\lambda^{2}+\lambda \lambda^{\prime}+\mu \lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
\times \exp \left[-\frac{1}{2} t\left(\lambda^{\prime}+3 \mu+2 \lambda\right.\right. \\
\left.\left.-\sqrt{\lambda^{\prime 2}-2 \lambda^{\prime} \mu+\mu^{2}+4 \lambda \mu}\right)\right] \\
\left(2 \mu^{2}+2 \mu \lambda^{\prime}+\lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu+\lambda \lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
\times\left[\sqrt{\lambda^{\prime 2}-2 \lambda^{\prime} \mu+\mu^{2}+4 \lambda \mu}+2\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)\right] \\
\times\left[\mu\left(2 \mu^{2}+2 \mu \lambda^{\prime}+\lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu+\lambda \lambda^{\prime}\right)\right] \\
\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)\left(-\mu^{2}+\lambda^{2}+\lambda \lambda^{\prime}+\mu \lambda^{\prime}\right. \\
\left.+\mu \sqrt{\lambda^{\prime 2}-2 \lambda^{\prime} \mu+\mu^{2}+4 \lambda \mu}\right) \\
\times \exp \left[-\frac{1}{2} t\left(\sqrt{\lambda^{\prime 2}-2 \lambda^{\prime} \mu+\mu^{2}+4 \lambda \mu}\right.\right. \\
\left.\left.+\lambda^{\prime}+3 \mu+2 \lambda\right)\right] \\
\left(2 \mu^{2}+2 \mu \lambda^{\prime}+\lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu+\lambda \lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
\times\left[\sqrt{\lambda^{\prime 2}-2 \lambda^{\prime} \mu+\mu^{2}+4 \lambda \mu}+2\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)\right] \\
\times\left[\mu\left(2 \mu^{2}+2 \mu \lambda^{\prime}+\lambda^{2}+2 \lambda \mu+\lambda \lambda^{\prime}\right)\right]
\end{gathered}
$$

Similarly, it is possible to quantify $P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)$ and $P_{0}(t)$.
It could be useful to quantify, for each state $j$ of the system, the probability $P_{j}(t)$ in the case of stationary conditions, i.e.,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{j}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=0
$$

As a consequence, the generic condition explained by the Eq. 8.25 becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{i}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t} & =\sum_{j \in\{\text { state IN } j\}} P_{j}(t) t_{j}-\sum_{k \in\{\text { state OUT } j\}} P_{i}(t) t_{k} \\
& =0
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, for the previously introduced differential equations,

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{0}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=0=\mu P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)-P_{0}(t)\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=0=\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right) P_{0}(t)-(\lambda+\mu) P_{\mathrm{I}}(t) \\
+2 \mu P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=0=\lambda P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)-2 \mu P_{\mathrm{II}}(t) \\
P_{0}(t)+P_{\mathrm{I}}(t)+P_{\mathrm{II}}(t)=1
\end{array}\right.
$$

i.e.,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P_{0}(t \rightarrow \infty)=2 \mu^{2} \frac{2 \mu^{2}+2 \mu\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)+\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)}{\left[\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)\right]^{2}} \\
& P_{\mathrm{I}}(t \rightarrow \infty)=2 \mu \frac{2 \mu^{2}+2 \mu\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)+\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)}{\lambda^{2}\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)} \\
& P_{\mathrm{II}}(t \rightarrow \infty)=\frac{2 \mu^{2}+2 \mu\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)+\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda^{\prime}\right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

These results are true in the case of asymptotic values of availability and unavailability. The applications of the Markov chain modeling and analysis illustrated so far are a few examples of the power and effectiveness of this set of tools. Other advanced applications are presented in the literature and are not subject of this book.

### 8.10 Common Mode Failures and Common Causes

The assumption of independency of failures among different components within a production system is sometimes violated. Some components can share the same power source or external environmental conditions. This is the reason why in FTA, given a top event, it is possible to identify several identical basic events, and mirror events were properly introduced in the numerical examples illustrated in Sects. 8.5 and 8.7. How should we consider a MCS with two or more different basic components subject to common mode failures (also called "common causes")?

Fig. 8.111 Markov chain, common cause and a 2-dim MCS

A common cause can be modeled as a repairable event based on constant failure and repair rates. In particular, if we call them $c$ and $b$, respectively, the density function for the common cause event $w_{c \_c a u s e}(t)$ by the application of Eq. $5.95^{2}$ is

$$
w_{c \_c a u s e}(t)=\frac{c b}{c+b}+\frac{c^{2}}{c+b} \exp [-(c+b) t]
$$

The asymptotic value is
$w_{c \_c a u s e}(\infty)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}\left[w_{c \_c a u s e}(t)\right]=\frac{c b}{c+b} \underset{i \in 1 / c \geqq 1 / b}{\cong} c$.

If a MCS is made up of two or more basic events subject to common causes, Eq. 8.12 cannot be applied. For example, in presence of a cut set made up of two repairable components subject to a common cause of rates $(\lambda, \mu)=(c, b)$ it is possible to introduce the Markov chain as in Fig. 8.111.

### 8.10.1 Unavailability of a System Subject to Common Causes

The object of this section is to present an analytical model for the determination of the unavailability of a system with two or more components subject to common causes.

[^0]For this purpose consider a MCS made of two components A and B , modeled as $\left(\lambda_{i}, \mu_{i}\right)$ with $i=$ $1, \ldots, n$ and $n=2$, subject to a common cause modeled as $(c, b)$ and the following events:

1. There are no common cause events in $(0, t)$.
2. The last common cause event occurs in $(u-\mathrm{d} u, u]$, where $u \in(0, t)$.
The MCS can be considered as a redundant parallel system of components A and B. As a consequence, the unavailability of the system is the result of two different contributions:
3. Hypothesis I. The system unavailability is the result of the application of Eq. 8.12 when components A and B are supposed to be in a state of function for $t=0$, i. e., $(0,0)_{t=0}$. The probability of components A and B being in a state of failure in $t$ is

$$
\prod_{i=1}^{2} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) t}\right)
$$

Equation 8.66 does not consider the event "no common cause in $[0, t]$." The probability of no common causes in the system during $[0, t]$ is quantified by the basic equation (Eq. 5.27) as follows:

$$
\mathrm{e}^{-c t}
$$

As a consequence, the system unavailability assuming hypothesis I is

$$
Q_{1, S}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-c t} \prod_{i=1}^{2} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) t}\right)
$$

2. Hypothesis II. Assuming configuration $(1,1)_{u}$, Eq. 5.82 can be applied ${ }^{3}$ to quantify the probability of components A and B remaining in $(1,1)_{t}$ :

$$
\prod_{i=1}^{2}\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}+\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}} \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right)(t-u)}\right)
$$

Consequently, Eq. 8.69 differs from Eq. 5.82 because of the swapping of terms $\lambda$ and $\mu$.

[^1]
[^0]:    ${ }^{2}$ See also Table 5.6.

[^1]:    ${ }^{3}$ A new failure event is introduced: the failure rate is $\mu$ and the repair rate is $\lambda$ and Eq. 5.82 is applied.The probability of a common cause event occurring in $(u-\mathrm{d} u, u]$ is

$$
w_{c_{-} \text {cause }}(u) \mathrm{d} u \underset{\text { Eq. } 8.65}{\cong} c \mathrm{~d} u
$$

Hypothesis II is based on the assumption that the last common cause occurs in $(u-\mathrm{d} u, u]$. In particular, the probability that the system stays in $(1,1)$ during the period $[u, t]$ can be quantified similarly to Eq. 8.67:

$$
\mathrm{e}^{-c(t-u)}
$$

By Eqs. 8.69-8.71 the probability of components A and B remaining in the state of failure $(1,1)$ in $t$ as in $(1,1)_{u}$, because it is subject to a common cause between $(u-\mathrm{d} u, u]$, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{\mathrm{II}, S}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} c & \mathrm{e}^{-c(t-u)}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{2} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\right. \\
& \left.+\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}} \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right)(t-u)}\right) \mathrm{d} u
\end{aligned}
$$

As a consequence, the system unavailability, i. e., the probability of components A and B being in a state of failure in $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{S}(t)= & Q_{\mathrm{I}, S}(t)+Q_{\mathrm{II}, S}(t) \\
= & \mathrm{e}^{-c t} \prod_{i=1}^{2} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) t}\right) \\
& +\int_{0}^{t} c \mathrm{e}^{-c s}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{2} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\right. \\
& \left.\quad+\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}} \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) s}\right) \mathrm{d} s
\end{aligned}
$$

In general, for a MCS made of $n$ components subject to a common cause,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{S}(t)= & \mathrm{e}^{-c t} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) t}\right) \\
+ & \int_{0}^{t} c \mathrm{e}^{-c s}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\right. \\
& \left.\quad+\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}} \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) s}\right) \mathrm{d} s
\end{aligned}
$$

If $c=0$,

$$
Q_{S}(t, c=0)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) t}\right)
$$

This is the result of the application of Eqs. 5.83 and 8.12 .

### 8.10.2 Numerical Example, Dependent Event

Consider the application illustrated in Sect. 8.6.1 and the hypothesis that there is a common cause between the basic components/events A and B. Then the value of $c$ is supposed to be 0.2 year $^{-1}$ (five events per year). By the application of the Eq. 8.74 for $T=8,000 \mathrm{~h}$, when the system operates 365 days per year and 24 h per day, ${ }^{4}$ the unavailability is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& Q_{S}(8,000)=\mathrm{e}^{-c t} \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) t}\right) \\
& \quad+\int_{0}^{t} c \mathrm{e}^{-c s}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}}+\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}} \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu_{i}\right) s}\right) \mathrm{d} s \\
& =\mathrm{e}^{-2.28 \times 10^{-5} \times 8,000} \frac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{2 \times 10^{-5}+10^{-2}} \\
& \quad \times\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(2 \times 10^{-5}+10^{-2}\right) 8,000}\right) \frac{10^{-5}}{10^{-5}+5 \times 10^{-2}} \\
& \quad \times\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(10^{-5}+5 \times 10^{-2}\right) 8,000}\right) \\
& +\int_{0}^{t} 2.28 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{e}^{-2.28 \times 10^{-5} s} \\
& \quad \times\left[\left(\frac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{2 \times 10^{-5}+10^{-2}}+\frac{10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-5}+10^{-2}}\right)\right. \\
& \left.\quad \times\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\left(2 \times 10^{-5}+10^{-2}\right) s}\right)\right] \\
& \quad \times\left[\left(\frac{10^{-5}}{10^{-5}+5 \times 10^{-2}}+\frac{5 \times 10^{-2}}{10^{-5}+5 \times 10^{-2}}\right)\right. \\
& \left.\quad \times\left(\mathrm{e}^{-\left(10^{-5}+5 \times 10^{-2}\right) s}\right)\right] \mathrm{d} s
\end{aligned}
$$

${ }^{4} c=0.2$ year $^{-1}=0.2 /(24 \times 365) h^{-1} \sim 2.28 \times 10^{-5}$.$$
\begin{aligned}
= & 3.9999 \times 10^{-7}+2.2850 \times 10^{-5} \\
& \times \int_{0}^{8,000} \mathrm{e}^{\left(-2.28 \times 10^{-5}+2 \times 10^{-5}+10^{-2}+10^{-5}+5 \times 10^{-2}\right) s} \mathrm{~d} s \\
= & 3.9999 \times 10^{-7}+2.2850 \times 10^{-5} \int_{0}^{8,000} \mathrm{e}^{-6 \times 10^{-2} s} \mathrm{~d} s
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
=3.9999 \times 10^{-7}+2.2850 \times 10^{-5} & \frac{1}{6 \times 10^{-2}} \\
& \times\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\left(6 \times 10^{-2}\right) 8,000}\right) \\
= & 3.81 \times 10^{-4}
\end{aligned}
$$

This value differs from $q_{\mathrm{AB}}$ quantified in Sect. 8.6.1 and also influences the system availability in $T=$ 8,000 h.# Basic Models and Methods for Maintenance of Production Systems
